Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The seed mixtures for the seeding consisted of seed that was available at the time and seed left over from other seedings since this was the last seeding to be approved for the extremely busy season. Therefore, many of the seed mixtures contained small quantities of seed not originally planned for House Creek. The project was divided into six areas to cover different prescriptions for the variation in soil types, precipitation and other needs. Some were combined during seeding due to lack of seed.

In the first year, wind erosion would increase slightly on the treatment areas compared to the protection only and no action alternatives because of the added surface disturbance caused by drilling. However, by the end of two years, grazing tolerant, fire resistant vegetation would be established on the treatment areas, and long-term soil stability would be much improved over either of the alternatives. Within three years, a 50-60% canopy cover is expected. By the end of four growing seasons, soil cover would be essentially complete, and bare ground would be much reduced compared to the pre-burn vegetation on the treated areas. Pollution and sedimentation of the Cedar Creek Reservoir would be much reduced compared to the two alternatives. The sediment would be trapped in the Black Canyon and Rocky Canyon drainages. Wind and water erosion on existing seedings would be minimal.

On the drilled treatment areas, a mixture of perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs will be established rather than a predominance of cheatgrass. The perennial grasses which have been emphasized in the seed mix will be compatible with existing seeded grasses. Intermediate wheatgrass has been emphasized on suitable sites where it would be used during the summer. Crested wheatgrass has been emphasized where use is predominantly in spring and fall. The fourwing saltbush would restore a shrub component which would be valuable both for late summer cattle grazing and for winter deer grazing. The alfalfa would enrich the dietary protein content of both livestock and wildlife, especially during the critical late summer period. A low incidence of reburns would be maintained, further depletion of perennial species would be prevented, and big sagebrush could return in time to provide wildlife habitat. Overstocking and low vigor of perennial grasses based upon
drastic increases in cheatgrass production would be prevented. Forage production would be greatly increased compared to pre-burn levels.

On the aerially seeded wildlife habitat areas, sagebrush canopy cover and suitable stand height would be reestablished far more rapidly and uniformly than natural successions and variability in sagebrush seed survival would allow. The crucial mule deer wintering habitat and sage grouse nesting and brooding habitat would be out of production for a much shorter period. The Magnar wildrye, because of its tall stature, would enhance wildlife cover as well as forage availability. The burnet, alfalfa, and pubescent wheatgrass would greatly improve crude protein availability for pregnant mule deer does in early spring on a major wintering area.

The proposed action would allow existing seedings to regain their vigor, with little long-term impact upon plant density or productivity. Minor areas of burned native range would have an increased composition of cheatgrass.

Because of limitations of time and equipment availability and delays caused by the budgetary process, this seeding will probably not be completed before May 1, 1986. While this greatly increases the probability of seeding failure, the project is located in a 12+ inch precipitation area, and has a better chance of growing season moisture and ultimate success than any of the other Jarbidge RA fire rehabilitation plans for 1985 fires. Failure to seed will result in a vegetation, i.e., cheatgrass, which will meet only one of the special objectives of this plan and will irreversibly foreclose future range management and wildlife habitat options.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Exceptional September rainfall in 1985 followed by exceptional rainfall and warm temperatures in late January, February, and early March, 1986, created exceptional conditions for spring cheatgrass germination and growth before drilling could begin. Deep-furrow drills were not available in adequate numbers, and, indeed, standard rangeland drills were not available in adequate numbers due to a large fire year in 1985 throughout the Intermountain area. For this reason grain drills had to be substituted for standard rangeland drills, Rangeland drills and especially the grain drills were not capable of removing adequate cheatgrass competition from the vicinity of the drill rows to allow use of the soil moisture by the seeded species.

April and May, 1986 were drier than normal and late May and early June were unseasonably warm, with temperatures in the 100s. It was apparent as early as July 1986, that the seeding had failed on the flatter basins and drainage bottoms where cheatgrass was abundant prior to the fire, while it was successful on uplands with sparse cheatgrass, particularly on north and east slopes. Thundershowers may have been a major factor in the success of those areas which did develop. Several years of below normal precipitation and unfavorable temperatures beginning in 1987 have greatly suppressed the cheatgrass on the failed portions of the 1985 seeding. The area now has much bare soil with a sparse mat of old weathered cheatgrass litter. The cheatgrass vegetation was not meeting either the original EFR objectives or Land Use Plan Objectives for the area. Now an opportunity to successfully replace the cheatgrass vegetation is at hand. Similar successful reseeding were done in the fall of 1977 on long-term cheatgrass areas which had been burned in the Bicentennial Fire on 1976 and had failed to germinate in 1977 due to severe drought.

Specific Objectives
1. Provide long-term soil stability with a perennial canopy cover of 50-60% within three years on 7700 acres of public land. The canopy cover should consist of perennial grasses and forbs.
Needs: Practically all of the proposed seeding area was dominated by cheatgrass after the failure of the initial rehabilitation attempt. Scattered alfalfa and crested wheatgrass did establish, but not in sufficient amounts to suppress the annuals. Some natural sagebrush recruitment has also occurred. Much of the soil surface is now bare or with a sparse cover of old cheatgrass litter. A permanent perennial ground cover is needed to protect these sites during periodic droughts.

2. Provide a greater diversity of plant species in the area consisting of perennial grasses and forbs within three years.
Needs: This burn lies in Multiple Use Area 7 (See Ecological Condition II.A.) A lack of species diversity characterizes the cheatgrass burn which is basically a three species community consisting of cheatgrass with lesser amounts of squirreltail and Sandberg bluegrass. Seedings should improve species diversity and site stability and increase multiple-use management options.

3. Reduce fire hazard by reducing the composition of annual grasses. Establish a perennial vegetation canopy cover of 50-60% within three years.
Needs: Annual plants species dominate this area and have the potential of reburning every 2-5 years as has been observed in similar areas in this vicinity. A perennial plant community is needed to prevent the complete dominance of the site by annuals.

Objectives: The objective of this treatment was to prevent erosion by reducing bare ground with a drill seeding of perennial grasses.  The specific objective is that by the end of the third growing season following treatment that there will be a density of at least 1.5 plants/m2 within the treatment area.
Planned_Implementation:
Ground seeding would primarily be done in those areas that prior to the fire contained sagebrush and antelope bitterbrush, these areas burned at a higher fire severity than other portions of the burn. The site had a scattered canopy of yellow rabbitbrush and antelope bitterbrush, and was dominated by basin big sagebrush with intermixed islands of Wyoming
big sagebrush and little sagebrush. The site had a perennial herbaceous understory containing bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue, crested wheatgrass, Thurber’s needlegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, Cusick’s bluegrass and Sandbergs bluegrass.
Approximately 3,500 acres of public land in the burned area would be seeded using rangeland drills during the fall of 2012 or spring of 2013 with a mixture of native and non-native perennial grasses and big sagebrush species. Evaluation of suitability for seeding occurred over the entire burned area using data collected in preparation of an Order 3 Soil Survey and Ecological Site Inventory. This data was primarily collected in 2007 and was used to determine pre-burn ecological condition and vegetative composition. Areas which were in late-potential natural communities (PNC's) ecological status were not considered for ground seeding, because they were determined to be at a lower risk for conversion to a system dominated by annual invasive grasses. Vegetation communities in late-PNC seral stage express a mosaic of species composition and structure consistent with site potential and should meet the objectives of the LUP. 
Most of the burn area is at a moderate risk for cheatgrass conversion. The site is moderately to highly suited for seeding using the rangeland drill, but prior treatments in the burn area have been successful. Areas not suited for rangeland seeding were identified and were not considered for treatment. Seed would be applied using rangeland drills which would be trailed by a cultipacker to compress the sagebrush seed into the soil surface. An additional 200 acres would be seeded using a UTV seeder during the fall of 2012 or the spring of 2013. 
Two seed mixes have been designed for the Danner Loop 2 fire; they will contain bluebunch wheatgrass, snake river wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Idaho fescue, bottlebrush squirreltail, Thurber’s needlegrass, Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron sibericum), and crested wheatgrass. The two seed mixes are a strictly native mix and a non-native/native mix. The non-native/native mix will contain crested wheatgrass and/or Siberian wheatgrass, bluebunch wheatgrass and/or Snake River wheatgrass, and Idaho fescue with bottlebrush squirreltail completing the seed mix. This mix will primarily be used in existing land treatment areas. However, there will be approximately 200 acres of native range which will be seeded using the non-native/native mix. Cheatgrass and medusahead rye have been spreading into this area from adjacent private land, and the potential expansion of these annual invasive grasses into the rest of the burn area is a concern of the IDT. The native mix will contain bluebunch wheatgrass and/or snake river wheatgrass, Idaho fescue and bottlebrush squirreltail with certain areas being selected for seeding with Thurber’s needlegrass. The use of locally collected seed exists for bottlebrush squirreltail, Thurber’s needlegrass and bluebunch wheatgrass. Although some of this seed is currently available, additional seed is currently in production under contract grow out and will be available this fall, assuming that the seed meets contract specifications. The demand for native seed on this project and others on the
Vale District exceeds the capacity of the native plant program so additional seed for these species will be acquired through other sources, like the Boise Seed Warehouse.
Actual_Implementation: The drill seeding was implemented in December 2012 and into January of 2013.  The seed mixes utilized on this project are listed at the end of this table.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
S-2 Ground Seeding
The specific objective of the ground seeding treatment is that by the end of the third growing season following treatment that the density of deep rooted perennial grasses (seeded or natural recovery) will be at least 1.5 plants/m2.  Two seed mixes were utilized as shown above in Part 5.

In FY13 a total of 3 vegetation monitoring plots were established to measure plant germination and density within the seeding areas.  

Results of the monitoring indicate that current density as measured in FY 13 is 2.5 plants/m2.

Data measured in FY 14 indicate that average total cover was 66% inside the burn area
and 78.6% outside the burn area. This equates to a 84% similarity. Based on this data
the objective for these two treatments has been achieved.
2015 monitoring by Range personnel found that the success of regrowth was adequate for
the return of grazing and grazing was resumed.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The area burned by the Danner Loop 2 Fire is in need of treatment to ensure desirable vegetation will stabilize the site and prevent invasion by annual grasses and noxious weeds. This can be met by seeding competitive perennial vegetation on 3,716 acres and planting approximately 1030 acres of sagebrush and antelope bitterbrush seedlings. The treatment area will be closed to livestock grazing. This closure will allow for the rehabilitated area to be rested from grazing for one full year and through a second growing season at a minimum, or until monitoring data or professional judgment indicate that the health and vigor of desired vegetation has recovered to levels adequate to support and protect upland function. The minimum two growing season closure will be in effect until BLM personnel determine that residual perennial plant species have reached adequate levels of recovery to re-authorize livestock grazing use. Construction of ten miles of temporary fencing is needed to protect the burn area, minimize soil movement, and reduce the invasion of undesirable annual plants and noxious weeds. A cattleguard will also need to be installed along the Lower Cow Lakes Road. The site will be inventoried for the establishment of noxious weeds. If found, they would be treated in accordance with national and district guidelines for noxious weed treatment.

Two seed mixes have been designed for the Danner Loop 2 fire; they will contain bluebunch wheatgrass, snake river wheatgrass (Elymus wawawaiensis), Idaho fescue, bottlebrush squirreltail, Thurber’s needlegrass, Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron sibericum), and crested wheatgrass. The two seed mixes are a strictly native mix and a non-native/native mix. The non-native/native mix will contain crested wheatgrass and/or Siberian wheatgrass, bluebunch wheatgrass and/or Snake River wheatgrass, and Idaho fescue with bottlebrush squirreltail completing the seed mix. Objectives:
The specific objectives of the proposed action would be to replace the existing annual vegetation
and restore adapted perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs. In addition, the establishment of
perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs is expected to reduce wildland fire frequency and associated
suppression costs and allow more natural ecological functions to occur.
Planned_Implementation:
The Fall following the burn and spray treatment, the treated area would be seeded with a
mixture of adapted perennial grasses, forbs and shrubs. Both native and nonnative seed
mixes would be utilized. Native plants would be used to the extent possible in areas
which retain remnant native herbaceous species and have the potential for reestablishment
of native species with available plant material. Based on availability and site suitability,
species may include the following: bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, great
basin wildrye, Lewis flax, western yarrow, scarlet globemallow, big sagebrush, four-wing
saltbrush or other adapted natives. The perimeter of these treatment blocks may be lined
with strips from 100 to 300 feet (greenstripping) with nonnative species more resistant to
wildfire to break up fuel continuity and protect these areas from future wildfire and
reinvasion by annual weedy species. Nonnative plants will be used in areas that are more
heavily infested with invasive annual species, in areas where suitable adapted natives are
5
not available, and in areas to provide fuel breaks to reduce the size, spread and
occurrence of wildfire both in wildland urban interface areas and transitional areas
adjacent to more intact shrub habitat. Species mixtures may include plants such as
crested wheatgrass, great basin wildrye, bluegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, forage kochia,
four-wing saltbrush and big sagebrush. Depending upon individual species' seeding
requirements, the seeding/planting would be done using a rangeland drill and/or broadcast
application. Anticipated native and nonnative seed mix areas are identified on map 3. As

reducing the re-establishment of annual grasses and weeds, through seeding adapted nonnative

established crested wheatgrass seedings that were burned after seed ripe the first year if
vigor and health of the seeding has recovered by that time.

selected areas in the plant community.
Planned_Implementation: The proposed action would be to seed approximately 1,500 acres of the Jordan Creek\r\nFire and 33,787 total acres in the Jackies Butte Fire for a total of 35,287 acres with a\r\nnon-native seed mix using rangeland drills
Actual_Implementation: Drilled 35,287 acres for an average cost of $16.49/acre.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
During the summer of 2004 the rehabilitation project was monitored to determine success of
seeding efforts, weed infestations, and the recovery of areas burned, but unseeded. Sixteen
different areas were monitored within the rehab area of which 13 are located on the Jackie Butte
Fire and 3 are located on the Jordan Creek Fire. At each area, one transect of 25 plots was taken
with a 3 foot diameter hoop. At each plot the number of seeded plants and natural regenerating
plants were recorded, as well as the presence or absence of noxious weeds.
Monitoring results for 2004 showed exceptional regeneration in all areas burned, including
seeded and non-seeded areas. Of the three transects on the Jordan Creek Fire, 14% of the
monitoring sites had 1-5 plants existing. Of the 13 sites monitored on the Jackie Butte Fire, 10%
had 1-5 seeded grass plants and 1% had 6 or more seeded grass plants. In all 16 sites monitored
no sagebrush seedlings were found.
To date, the success of the seeded areas is poor. We determined if over half the plots in one
transect had 6 or more plants the seeding would be considered successful. At best there were
only 3 plots that had hits in the “6 or more” category. Some of these seedlings will not survive
to be mature plants. We have been in a drought the last several years which may account for the
poor germination; however we need to continue monitoring for another year to determine the
effectiveness of the treatment type.
What didn’t work: Seeding
Lessons learned: Drought was considered the biggest factor in the success/failure of the areas we
seeded. Also the time of year seed was set into the ground. Lawsuits delayed implementation of
the seeding contract until late December. Ground conditions were unfavorable for seeding at
that time. Our monitoring data was consistent in showing that native and non-native grass
species that were established before the fire re-established themselves. This is what monitoring
showed uniformly over the entire rehab area.

About 3,000 acres of critical mule deer habitat was burned by the fire.
Much of this is on private and State land but about 480 acres of BLM administered
land important as deer winter range was burned.
The primary browse species in the area are bitterbrush and serviceberry.
More important deer winter range is located east of Shoshone Creek, out
of the fire area. Both the eastern unburned area and the burned area
provide year round range for local deer and winter range for higher
elevation deer populations of both Idaho and Northern Nevada.
Also within the burned area, habitat for sage grouse was destroyed.

last decade there has been a steady decline in numbers. Numerous sage
grouse strutting grounds formerly occupied by 50-60 males are now used
by only 6-10 males.
Confirmed and unconfirmed reports of a total of about 20 deer killed by
the fire have been received. Idaho Fish and Game Department personnel
have photographs showing sage grouse killed by the fire.
The U. S. Forest Service has already devised plans for restoring wildlife
habitat destroyed by fire on the land they administer., In all certainty,
wildlife habitat losses will not be recognized in the rehabilitation of
State and private lands, thus adding even more importance to restoring
wildlife habitat on BLM-administered lands.
Rehabilitation of wildlife habitat in the BLM-administered area should
have two objectives: (1) restore shrub species in areas significant as
winter deer habitat&* and (2) attempt to determine successful species
and methods of propagation that could be used with confidence on other
crucial areas that will surely burn in the future. Lack of seed sources
or planting stock will limit the various species that should be used.
On those areas where fire completely removed the sagebrush, there is
no reason to consider forbs or legumes for sage grouse except on those
burned areas contiguous to remaining sage stands. In these areas,
Ladak or nomad alfalfa would be beneficial for sage grouse and other
wildlife species, providing subsequent livestock use of the area could
be managed closely enough to permit establishment and maintenance of
the alfalfa.
For rehabilitation of deer habitat it is recommended that 200 acres in
the S~, 833, T15S, R16E.,BH be seeded at the rate of three pounds of
bitterbrush and four pounds of yellow sweet clover per acre. It is
also believed cliff rose will do well in this area. About nine acres
should be seeded at the rate of three pounds of cliff rose and four
pounds of yellow sweet clover per acre.
Prior to planting, the bitterbrush seed should be treated with various
chemicals to repel rodents and birds. A mixture of 0.5 percent Endrin,
2.0 percent Arasan, and a coating of aluminum powder should be used.
- A diluted latex solution serves as an adherent. After treatment, the
seed should be allowed to dry before planting. The sweet clover should
be inoculated with nitrogen-fixing bacteria prior to planting.
The area planted should be fenced to exclude all livestock use for
perhaps as long as three years. Livestock use should be carefully
controlled as to time and amount of use subsequent to establishment
of the browse species. This should not be too difficult to achieve with
the highly productive 5l,OOO-acre Berger Resource Conservation Area so
closely adjacent to the burned area.

Objectives: Drill seed desirable perennial vegetation in order to compete with medusahead, an invasive annual\r\ngrass, and accelerate recovery within the burn perimeter.
Planned_Implementation:
This treatment consists of drill seeding 7078 acres on the Riley Field Fire (Map 9). The seeding will be done utilizing rangeland drills. Seeding will occur in the winter/spring of 2015/2016. A desirable non-native seed mix comprised of crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum), forage kochia (Bassia prostrate) and Ladak alfalfa (Medicago sativa) will be utilized in order to compete with the moderate to heavy infestation of medusahead. Plant guides can be found in the Attachments. These species were selected by the I.D. team which include ODFW and USFWS: 1) given the sites risk for invasive annual grass
establishment, 2) the potential to reduce the risk of an increased fire frequency to protect and assist in the reestablishment of key plant species such as sagebrush by maintaining ecologic functions, and 3) the low potential for native seed survival in ecological sites that support Wyoming big sagebrush steppe communities and are at risk to invasive annual grasses (James et al. 2011; Davies et al. 2011; and Dr. Kirk Davies preliminary results with study sites near the Riley Field Fire comparing native to non-native germination and establishment of deep rooted bunchgrasses in treated medusahead sites). This treatment will
take place one year post-aerial weed treatment application Crested wheatgrass possesses a deep root system with early growth giving it an advantage when competing in an area threatened by annual grasses. The drought tolerance, fibrous
root systems, good seedling vigor, and ability to quickly stabilize soils and slow runoff makes this species ideal for rehabilitation in areas with low-moderate annual precipitation that is threatened by invasive annual grasses. Crested wheatgrass will fill in niche space created by the fire, however there are potential costs with the establishment of this plant into those open sites and that is a reduction in potential establishment of native long lived perennial bunch grasses such as blue bunch wheatgrass (Davies et al. 2011 ). This cost by using crested wheatgrass is outweighed by the threat of not being able to successfully occupy those open sites in the 2-3 year window before medusahead and cheatgrass either reclaim or invade and dominate the plant community (Young 1992; Davies et al. 2010; and Davies et al. 2011 ). This would result in a failed system that no longer provides the structure, function, and processes needed to allow plant community succession to move in a positive trajectory needed for wildlife habitat.
Forage Kochia has been shown to compete extremely well against aggressive, exotic annual weeds such as cheatgrass, Russian thistle and medusahead. Plantings of forage kochia can decrease densities of annual weeds, thus decreasing fire intervals of degraded rangelands while providing valuable forage to livestock, and forage and cover for wildlife and upland
game birds. While research is still very limited on forage kochia use by sage-grouse, observations of sage-grouse using forage kochia have been made (Waldron, 2002). Forage . kochia is also high in protein, testing at over 20% in July, which can help wildlife meet protein requirements later in the year (Smith, 2006).
Ladak alfalfa is a legume used in may desirable non-native seed mixes as a supplement for wildlife forage. Alfalfa is an excellent food for antelope, deer, elk, Canada goose, and sage and sharp tail grouse. It is fair food for sandhill crane, mallard, Hungarian partridge, and  pheasant. Additionally, it is relatively drought tolerant and does not easily burn during wildfire. This competes well against invasive annual grasses and is relatively fire resistant. Additionally, conversations with US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (ODFW) have indicated that in areas where invasive annual grasses are in danger of dominating the site and converting the area to an annual grassland thereby reducing biodiversity and habitat for wildlife species, they would support the use of desirable non-native species such as crested wheatgrass, forage kochia and Ladak alfalfa to prevent critical habitat loss (Sage-Grouse Specific Prioritization Criteria PDF in
Attachments). Planting Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings into crested wheatgrass seedings has been successful, and is planned for under ES Issue 2. Preventing the degradation of ecosystem functions by utilizing the non-native seed mix is the first priority. Without functioning systems, planting sagebrush will be unsuccessful.
Discs on the drills will be dropped to achieve full depth up to 3 inches; no chains will be pulled behind. This will leave the furrows created by the discs open and with clayey soils and rock discs will most often not penetrate more than 1/2 in to 1 in. This method has been used by private land owners and Burns District with good results. Proposed restoration activities especially those involving drill seeding are considered undertakings warranting review and compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. This work needs to be conducted in consultation with the State Historic Preservation Officer, affected Indian tribes and others as appropriate. BLM is developing specific plans for conducting archaeological survey and site identification services focusing on emergency stabilization of burned areas including ground seeding and aerial seeding where these  activities have the potential to affect cultural properties. It is estimated that 7078 acres of proposed ground seeding will require cultural resources inventory prior to drill seeding in the Riley Field Fire area. Cultural clearances will be conducted prior to seeding.

Objectives:
The objectives are to:
1. Establish a vegetative component of native species that coincides with the ecological site
descriptions for each seeded area.
2. To establish and enhance sage-grouse habitat that provides effective cover and forage for
brooding, leking and nesting activities.

Planned_Implementation:
The ELFO has identified approximately 5,000 acres for drill seeding this fall. Given the time
constraints and the lack of seed available seeding area will focus on Sage-grouse Priority
Habitat areas. Drill seed 5000 acres using rangeland drills and a TruAx drill. A smaller ATV
sized Dew Drop Drill Seeder will be used to drill seed 100 acres. Seeding will be conducted
in late fall prior to any predicted significant snowfall. Drilling will be accomplished by BLM
staff. Seeding areas have been mapped by BLM.
Due to the very rocky topography of the ELFO three different sized drill seeders will be
used. Two rangeland drills, a Truax drill and a Dew Drop, ATV sized drill. The ELFO
currently has two large Rangeland drills and a Truax drill. All three can be pulled by a rubber
tire tractor or a Caterpillar. A rubber tire tractor will be used when pulling a single drill and a
Caterpillar will be used when pulling tandem drills. Areas appropriate for using large drills
Rush - G5Z8 - 09/20/2012 - Page 21 of 69
were selected by close proximity to roads, which allows for large equipment access. Most
of these places are relatively flat with slopes less than 15 percent with moderately rocky
terrain and some rock outcrops.
The Dew Drop Drill is a small drill seeder that can be pulled behind an ATV or UTV vehicle.
The ELFO is requesting the purchase of one of these drills in order to seed areas where the
larger rangeland drills cannot access or maneuver. Drill seeding at this scale will allow the
ELFO to include areas with slopes greater than 15 percent and to maneuver between the
many talus slopes and rock outcrops that are prevalent in this region.
Drill seeding will occur in areas that have been identified by ELFO personnel as appropriate
for this activity. There are three general sagebrush variation systems identified as requiring
soil stabilization, these sites are spread throughout the fire perimeter. The type of drill used
in seeding will be very site specific.
Mountain sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata var. vaseyana) communities are generally located
in elevations above 2,600 feet. Species to be seeded in these areas include Mountain big
sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata var. vaseyana), antelope bitterbrush (Prushia tridentata),
bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Idaho fescue (Festuca Idahoensis) and
hawksbeard (crepis sp.) Within the perimeter of the Rush Fire six areas have been identified,
and encompass 2052 acres located in T35, R17, Sec. 25; T35, R18, Sec. 25, 32; T34, R18,
Sec. 5, 8, 11, 14, 23. In these areas it is estimated that 1000 acres will be seeded with the
rangeland drills.
Basin big (Artemisia tridentata var. tridentata) communities are generally located at elevations
ranging from 1,900 to 6,900 feet and are often found in valleys comprised of deep soils.
Species to be seeded in these areas include Basin big (Artemisia tridentata var. tridentata),
antelope bitterbrush (Prushia tridentata), bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata),
Great Basin wild rye (Leymus cinereus) and yarrow (Achillea millafolium). Within the

located in T32, R16, Sec. 21, 22, 28; T31, R16, Sec. 23. In these areas it is estimated that
1200 acres will be seeded with the rangeland drills.
Wyoming sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata var. wyomingensis) communities are generally
located in lower to intermediate elevations ranging from 2,600 to 7,200 feet. This species
occurs in areas with shallower soils than Basin big varieties but can be found in the same
elevation bands. Species to be seeded in these areas include Wyoming big sagebrush
(Artemisia tridentata var. wyomingensis), antelope bitterbrush (Prushia tridentata),
bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus
elymoidies), Sandberg’s bluegrass (Poa secunda), and Lewis flax (Linum Lewisii). Within
the perimeter of the Rush Fire ten areas have been identified and encompass 4454 acres
located in T31, R17, Sec. 22,23,27,28; T30, 17, Sec. 28,29,30; T29, R18, Sec. 16, 17, 20,
21. In these areas it is estimated that 2600 acres will be seeded with the rangeland drills.

Objectives: Objective: To re-vegetate a burned and highly disturbed native rangeland area with essentially a native seed mixture of grasses and a shrub in order to stabilize the soils and maintain the area for the betterment of\r\nwildlife habitat and watershed enrichment.
Planned_Implementation: Drill seed grasses and forbs
Actual_Implementation: Implementation Monitoring: About 3,475 acres of the fire was drill seeded with a grass/shrub seed mix by contractor Greg Jarolimek of Filer, Idaho using five of his own rangeland drills. The seed was premixed by Shoshone operation staff with the assistance of the fire crew. The drill seeding operation was done in two phases because of a winter shutdown caused by frozen ground. The first phase of 934 acres was drilled into dry soils between November 18 and November 29, 2006. The second phase of the remaining 2,541 acres, was done in the spring of 2007 between March 17 and April 7, and was done when soils were moist.\r\n\r\nIn November of 2006 a grass/shrub seed mix was drill seeding in 934 acres of the burn. In the spring of 2007 the remaining 2,541 acres were drill seeded. The 2007 monitoring reports indicated that the seeding was off to a good start. Many of the seeded plants had germinated and were producing seed stalks. The drill seeded Wyoming sagebrush was less apparent, but still present. The drawback to this seeding was that most of the area was re-burned in 2007 by the Murphy Complex. In January of 2007 18,722 acres was aerial seeding with Wyoming sagebrush. In the summer of 2007 monitoring crews observed seedlings in the areas that had been seeded.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results: Inspection by the Shoshone Operation staff found this drill seeding project to have been successfully completed by the contractor to BLM specifications and completed as best and fast that it could based on weather conditions. For a first year analysis, by field surveys and study sites in mid July 2007, it
was determined and observed that the drill seeding on the 3,475 acre site of the middle area of the Sailor Cap Fire appeared to be off to a very good start for mostly the grasses. Lots of drill seeded grass plants had germinated, were making good growth and production, and many plants had developed some seed stalks.

Effectiveness Monitoring: Inspection of the jobs found that the work had been done effectively, the seed drilled in the proper areas and at the correct rates, and the entire job completed as best as weather would allow.
For a first year analysis, it was observed, by field surveys and transect studies installed at a few sites, that the drill seeding appears to be off to a very good start for mostly the grasses. Lots of drill seeded grass plants
had germinated, were making good growth and production, and many plants had developed some seed stalks. The observation of the seeded shrub of Wyoming sagebrush was less apparent, but there were a few to be seen. And most appeared to be healthy and doing well. Time will tell. The main drawback of all this
was that most of the drill seeding areas were re-burned again this year by the Murphy Complex fire, but pretty much at a light intensity for the most part. Next year's surveys will better tell conditions and results.

Objectives for the White Mule Fire Rehabilitation Plan are as follows:
1. Stabilize soils and reduce future fire hazards in cheatgrass dominated
areas by reducing the re-establishment of annual grasses and weeds, through
seeding adapted non-native species. Protect the rehabilitation effort by
excluding livestock grazing in the Dry Creek Pasture for at least two

for wildlife, increase effective precipitation by capturing and holding snow
during the winter months by establishing a deep rooted shrub component in
the plant community.

(Wyoming big sagebrush, bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail) via
seeding native perennial species.
4. Protect the seedings and burned area by reducing the Wild Horse
population numbers from 219 to between 50 and 75 animals to insure the
health and vigor of the remaining horses in the HMA.
5. Reduce future burned acreage by establishing a 200 foot green strip along
the northern perimeter and the two-track road bisecting the burned area.
The green strip would buffer weed invasion and most importantly, buffer
future wildland fire spread.
6. Restore the boundary fence for protection of the seedings and burned
area.
7. Repair the road damage for public access and decreased soil erosion.

On some drill-seeded areas \u201cAnatone\u201d Bluebunch Wheatgrass seed was substituted for \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass seed, and Sandberg\u2019s Bluegrass seed was substituted for \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass seed. Objectives: The primary objective is to seed burned areas at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion.  \r\nEstablish three to five seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.   Reduce bare ground within the burn to decrease chance of cheatgrass establishment.  Stabilize the site by protecting the soil and reducing wind and water erosion.  Enhance public safety by reducing driving hazards caused by blowing dust.
Planned_Implementation: Because of these risks coupled with moderate annual precipitation (8-10 inches), a mix of native species was selected.  Seed approximately 20,586 acres with a native drill seed mixture of \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass, Sandberg\u2019s Bluegrass, \u201cRimrock\u201d Indian Ricegrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and \u201cToe Jam\u201d Bottlebrush Squirreltail. \r\n\r\nDrill seed approximately 21,628 acres of moderate to high vegetation mortality and burn severity in order to maintain ecological stability, minimize invasion of cheatgrass and noxious weeds (bull thistle, hoary cress, and Canada thistle), and stabilize areas identified as having high wind erosion hazard in order to minimize topsoil loss and fugitive dust.  Seed mixes utilize species that are adapted to the sites and are detailed in the specification (part F).  To maximize probability of success, seed will be applied concurrent with fall/winter moisture period between October and December 2006.  First year effectiveness includes stabilization of the soil surface, reducing topsoil loss, improving soil infiltration of moisture, providing competition for invasive non-native species and replacing any organic litter which was consumed by fire.  First season vegetation establishment will be by perennial native and non-native grasses, shrubs and forbs.  It is expected that vegetation establishment will be successful on all sites although the presence or absence of timely moisture could be a limiting factor.  Treatment effectiveness will be monitored (see specification 15).  Specification 12, Cultural Resource Treatment Clearance, has been written to provide for cultural clearance on any ground disturbing activities.  Clearance will be obtained before any treatments proceed.
Actual_Implementation: The area received cultural clearance by BLM archeologists prior to treatment implementation. Drilling was implemented using both BLM personnel (with either BLM equipment or rented equipment) and contracted personnel.  Drill-seeded areas were widely separated.  On some drill-seeded areas \u201cAnatone\u201d Bluebunch Wheatgrass seed was substituted for \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass seed, and Sandberg\u2019s Bluegrass seed was substituted for \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass seed.  Exact determination of where modified seed mixtures were applied is not possible.  Seeding proceeded as ground conditions allowed.  Drilling was monitored to ensure disks were cutting into soil. Toward the end of December, the seeding area had accumulated about 4 inches of snow with some drifting.  Conditions were adequate to complete the project.  A project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

NOTE: Where monitoring summary refers to "see below&&, refer to the 2009 closeout summary.

The Native Drill Seeding was monitored using permanent modified Freqdens transects at eight separate locations widely distributed across the burn on disjunct drilled areas (monitoring plot WNND – 03 was established on a portion of the Winters burn in the Winnemucca District where these Native Drill seedings were implemented, and is not evaluated here.)  Density numbers may suggest whether the original or modified seed mixtures were applied at any specific monitoring location, but all species applied during the implementation are listed for every monitoring plot. 

Monitoring Results:
2007 – Success varied from location to location across the widely separated disjunct drill seedings, with the seeded patch monitored at WNND – 01 the least successful (density of 0.07 seeded species per square meter) and WNND – 03 the most successful (density of 7.96 seeded species per square meter.)  It important to note that at these two monitoring points (and in general across all the drill seeding monitoring plots) there appears to be an inverse relationship between the density of preexisting Sandberg’s Bluegrass and the germinating density of total seeded species.  The established community of Sandberg’s Bluegrass at WNND – 01 was recorded at 30.64 plants per square meter: at WNND – 03 Sandberg’s Bluegrass density was recorded at only 1.22.  These numbers constitute evidence that the presence of a dense community of Sandberg’s Bluegrass at any given location scheduled for drill seeding is likely to render that seeding ineffective. 
Density numbers recorded at individual monitoring plot locations are presented above for interpretation, but the large array of densities for all monitoring sites confounds convenient analysis.  Unknown environmental factors (in addition to preexisting Sandberg’s Bluegrass), could have influenced disparate results recorded at different monitoring locations.  For convenience, an amalgamation of some results may be desirable because eight of the nine monitoring locations were established on Loamy 8-10 inch range sites (the most common range site across the large drill-seeded area.)  To encourage a general understanding of drill seeding success on Loamy 8-10 inch range sites across the treated area, density numbers for all seeded species (only) at all monitoring locations, are averaged below.  
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding was approaching the lower end of the objective density of three plants per square meter after the first year of growth.  This average should be interpreted very cautiously, especially with regard to results for Snake River Wheatgrass and Bluebunch Wheatgrass; and for results for Big Bluegrass and seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass, since these species were substituted for each other on indeterminate seeded patches.  
The ninth monitoring plot for the Winters burn Native Drill Seeding (WNND – 10) was established on a Sandy 8-10 inch range site, so comparisons with other results are less useful.  On the sandy site, seeded species had exceeded the objective density of three to five plants per square meter by the end of the first monitoring season, with Indian Ricegrass making the greatest contribution.   The Crested Wheatgrass and Russian Wildrye recorded at WNND – 07 during the second and final monitoring years are probably “orphans” stuck in the drilling apparatus and unintentionally introduced into the site. 

2008 – On the sandy site seeded species continued to exceed the objective density of three to five plants per square meter by the end of the second monitoring season, with Thickspike Wheatgrass making the greatest contribution.  The trade-off of Indian Ricegrass for Thickspike Wheatgrass, which appeared to occur between the first and second year of monitoring is perplexing.  It is possible the Indian Ricegrass seedlings recorded the first year failed to establish and were replaced by slow-starting Thickspike Wheatgrass seedlings during the second year.  Misidentifications are unlikely because the same technician read the plots both years, and seedlings of these species are easy to differentiate.  Average densities for all Native Drill Seeding monitoring plots are presented below. 
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding remained relatively constant, still approaching the lower end of the objective density of three plants per square meter after the second year of growth.  

2009 – Average densities for all Native Drill Seeding monitoring plots are presented below. 
Total average densities for seeded species on drilled areas of Loamy 8-10 inch range sites indicate that “on average,” the drill seeding doubled in density the final year of monitoring, well exceeding the target density for total seeded species.  The numerous disjunct patches composing the Winters Native Drill Seeding are marked by subtle differences in environmental factors of soils, topography, and grazing history.  Under such divergent conditions, the drill seeding responded slightly differently over the three growing seasons on each seeded area. 
The Native Drill Seeding also exceeded the target density where it was applied on the Sandy 8-10 inch range site (WNND – 10). 
The native drill seed mixture included numerous species, including commonly seeded Big Bluegrass, Indian Ricegrass, Thickspike Wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, and rarely seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass and Bottlebrush Squirreltail.  Success of each seeded species varied on disjunct patches with environmental conditions.  The large number of species applied appears to have provided a built-in flexibility to the response of the mixture to variation of environmental conditions across treated areas.  Thickspike Wheatgrass and Indian Ricegrass were most successful on the sandy site.  Bluebunch Wheatgrass and Snake River Wheatgrass were most successful on loamy sites that may have been in better range condition prior to the burn.  The rarely seeded Sandberg’s Bluegrass and Bottlebrush Squirreltail were most successful on clayey sites that may have been in poorer range condition prior to the burn. 
The Winters Native Drill seeding was fully successful across wide areas, probably attributable to the numerous species with unique ecological tolerances that made up the seed mixture.

The high foliar cover within the Joint allotment is an anomaly and is likely due to low number and the location of the plots. Foliar cover fluctuated between years for most pastures, this is likely due to yearly fluctuations in precipitation, competition and other environmental factors, differences in the number of plots monitored throughout the five years of monitoring, and livestock grazing once resumed. The overall trend was an increase in perennial grass foliar cover for all but two pastures, Sands Basin 3 and Shares Basin 2 which had less than 1% decreases each. Perennial grass foliar cover has increased by 14.9% since 2016.
It is likely that portions of all pastures seeded with Drill Mix B were also drill seeded in either the 1960s or 1980s with introduced grass species such as crested wheatgrass. Planned_Implementation: Native Ground-based Seedings (See Seeding Map). Ground seeding is proposed using rangeland drill methods due to burn severity, soil type, and invasive annuals. The rangeland drills would allow grass, forb, and sagebrush seeds to be separated and/or mixed and seeded at different depths and rates as appropriate to seed type. Approximately 4,320 acres of moderately burned area with fewer native perennial root crowns remaining would be drill seeded using Wyoming big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata Nutt. subsp. wyomingensis, bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoroegneria spicata), Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda), bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) and sage-grouse preferred perennial forbs based on seed availability. The current proposed forb species are taper tip hawksbeard (Crepis acuminata), Wyeth's buckwheat (Eriogonum heracleoides), western yarrow (Achillea millefolium ), and gooseberryleaf globemallow (Sphaeralcea grossulariifolia). Seeded varieties and species may be adjusted based on seed availability.\r\nThis seeding mix is intended to boost cover of perennial native grasses, forbs, and sagebrush, and infill gaps between recovering plants. The seed mix will also provide competition with cheatgrass and medusahead rye. Establishment of fire resistant perennial grass species in the burned area is critical to interrupt the fire and invasive species cycle and protect adjacent sagebrush habitat.\r\nDrill seeding is planned to begin in early Fall 2018. If regrowth of existing perennial grasses and forbs occur, the total proposed ground seeding acres would be reduced to appropriate sizes. The size of treatment would be determined after the 2018 growing season by field visits and extensive mapping of recovering vs non-recovering areas within the burned area. Additionally, natural recovery success would be evaluated by species to determine if adjustments to proposed seed mixes are needed. For example, if Sandberg bluegrass recovers naturally it may be removed from the seed mix and the seed mixes will be adjusted appropriately.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Drill Mix 2
Drill Mix 2 was used in areas with higher potential for cheatgrass establishment; these areas also
contained past seedings that had poor establishment of seeded species and high cheatgrass cover
pre-fire. Areas seeded with Drill Mix 2 showed some establishment of seeded species as well as
recovery of on-site native plants and remnants of past seedings. Subsequent to the Kinyon Road
Fire, some past seedings responded well to additional rest and became better established. This
establishment was supplemented with the Kinyon Road drill seeding.
As with Drill Mix 1, use of depth bands tended to result in inconsistent burial and spotty
establishment. Sagebrush seedlings were observed during site visits by the fire ecologist. Patchy
distribution of sagebrush seedlings resulted in non-detection in belt transects.

MONITORING RESULTS
The fire ecologist examined the seeded areas on multiple dates in spring and summer 2013, 2014, and 2015.
Quantitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• For drill seed areas – establish seeded grasses at densities of 3 plants/m2, seeded forbs at 0.3 plants/m2, and 0.10 plants /m2 for shrubs (bitterbrush).
• For aerial grass and forb areas – establish seeded grasses and forbs at densities of 3 plants /m2 for grasses and 0.2 plants/m2 for forbs.
• For sagebrush aerial seed areas – 0.10 plants/m2.
• The amount of bare mineral soil (i.e., soil lacking cover of plants, litter, or biological soil crust) is within 10% of what would be expected for the site based on an adjacent unburned site or the ecological site description.
Qualitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• Most desired herbaceous perennial plants are producing seed.
• The plants must also have developed root systems that are extensive enough to provide soil stabilization and prevent uprooting when grazed, especially when soils are moist.

FY 17
Monitoring plots were revisited for the 5th year monitoring by Chicago Botanical interns in the summer of 2017. Qualitative assessments were completed and included a general plot description, species inventory, and photo documentation. For the 5th year monitoring year, seven plots were revisited for qualitative assessments. Plots visited include 001, 002, 004, 006, 009, 010, and 012.
The Kinyon Road rehabilitation can be addressed geographically, as the treatments were divided separately into the eastern and western burned areas. The focus of this summary will be on the west side, also known as the Bruneau Overlook area, as heavy noxious weed infestations and unsuccessful drill seedings here were concerning. Due to the good establishment of the drill seed treatments on the eastern side, attention and resources should be focused on the Bruneau Overlook area in future treatments.
On the eastern side of Kinyon, drill seedings were highly successful. Perennial grasses, particularly bluebunch wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass, dominate the landscape, and the bare ground among them supports a high diversity of forbs with relatively low cheatgrass establishment. Though sagebrush seedlings were either not found or found in extremely low amounts in these areas, many sagebrush islands were seen near monitoring points, and could potentially re-seed the area regardless of the success of shrub seedings. Invasive weeds such as rush skeletonweed, halogeton, and Russian thistle are present, but are not an imminent threat, especially considering the health and expanse of the perennial grasses. It would be valuable for future projects to assess why the eastern Kinyon plantings were so successful compared to the Bruneau Overlook area.
The Bruneau Overlook seeding treatments have been moderately successful but present several challenges. In some areas, drill-seeded perennial bunchgrass populations are vigorous and extensive with good forb diversity, but cheatgrass density is still high. Most areas on this side of the Kinyon fire are cheatgrass-Sandberg’s bluegrass dominated sites with low forb diversity, and drill-seeded perennials are not competing as well. Few to no sagebrush seedlings were seen across the area, and sagebrush islands were also rarer. Noxious and invasive weed populations also present a problem.
A main concern for this area is extremely dense invasive weed populations, particularly Russian thistle. The Bruneau Overlook area is being overtaken by this dominant weed, and full hillsides of robust Russian thistle were found near monitoring points (Photo 1). The eastern monitoring area also showed some large Russian thistle populations. Russian thistle is likely to continue dominating the Kinyon Road area unless significant control measures are taken. Rush skeletonweed is also present across the Kinyon Road fire area, though to a much lesser extent than the thistle. It has the potential to continue spreading and impeding the advancement of perennial bunchgrasses. Chemical treatments in the Bruneau Overlook area on Russian thistle and rush skeletonweed would be most efficient in stopping the spread of these two species, though mechanical treatments on extremely dense Russian thistle patches could also be valuable.
Kinyon Road Fire (G1CH) FY2022 Monitoring – 10th Year 33
Precipitation data is from the Twin Buttes and Horse Butte RAWS stations, which are northeast of the burned area and southwest of the burned area, respectively. Monitoring reports at the first, second- and third-year mark illuminate a trend towards higher precipitation following treatment years, along with later summer and fall rains. This factor may have contributed to higher weed establishment and lower drill seed success. Previous reports also mention soil movement that filled in drill rows and lessened the establishment rate at Bruneau Overlook sites. Compounding this was the inefficient depth band use on the shrub seedings, consequently the first three years of monitoring found no shrub establishment in the monitoring sites. Upon qualitative monitoring at the five-year mark, scattered immature Wyoming big sagebrush were found in only half of the monitoring sites for all of Kinyon. Multiple factors led to both the low shrub establishment throughout Kinyon and the partial success of drill seed treatments in Bruneau Overlook.

Objectives for aerial seeding are as follows:

2. Obtain 100% or greater perennial cover of the low potential perennial plant cover for the appropriate ecological site by the end of the third year following fire containment.

Monitoring Results
Percent Perennial Cover
Line point intercept (LPI) data was used to calculate the percent perennial cover of each AIM monitoring plot. For each AIM plot, the percent foliar cover calculated for each transect was averaged to arrive at an overall percent perennial cover for the plot.

The AIM monitoring crew recorded the number of seeded species and their age class within a 1 meter by 1 meter quadrant every 2.5 meters along a 25 meter transect. Planned_Implementation:
This treatment consists of drill seeding 6,038 acres in the Cinder Butte Fire area.
The seeding will be done utilizing a rangeland drill. Seeding will occur in the fall of
the year (fiscal year 2018 and potentially 2019 depending upon weather/time
constraints). Timing is planned with snowfall to provide insulation for the seed
during the winter months; as the snow melts in the spring it will provide moisture
the seeds need to germinate. Siberian wheatgrass and crested wheatgrass were
selected by the IDT as the main perennial bunchgrasses to be used and were
determined as the species to compete with cheatgrass and establish on these
ecological sites with low resistance and resilience based on the ecological
site description and conditions pre-fire and post fire. The Oregon GRSG Approved
Resource Management Plan Amendment (ARMPA) directs managers to not mix
crested wheatgrass with native grass species seed; that is why the crested/forage
kochia mix with no native species included was selected to hold the site and resist
annual invasive grasses. Forage kochia was selected for the seed mix to increase the
number of functional groups present on the site to promote ecological function. An
additional benefit is deer and pronghorn antelope can utilize kochia for protein
browse in the coming years prior to the timeframe when sagebrush could
establish. There are no native forbs in the seed mix. Trend monitoring completed
between 2012-2017 for emergency stabilization and rehabilitation (ESR) in the
Miller-Homestead and Buzzard Complex, in similar sites to Cinder Butte Fire
Treatment Units 4 and 7, has shown that both perennial and annual forb response
meet sage-grouse habitat objectives the first 1-3 growing seasons post fire.
Perennial forb species in the Northern Great Basin meristematic tissue are located
below ground and current year above ground production is dormant prior to the fire
season, which greatly reduces the risk of mortality from fire. This makes forbs less
vulnerable to wildland fire than perennial bunchgrasses that have meristematic
tissue at the soil surface that is often associated with an accumulation of litter
within the crown of the plant. Furthermore, high mortality rates on perennial
bunchgrasses are associated with > 15 percent shrub and tree cover on the landscape
whereas forbs are less vulnerable to these high severity conditions. Vegetation
monitoring will document the recovery (species and percent cover) of native forbs
in the area.
In Unit 4 there are two areas that total 1,730 acres where forage kochia will be
excluded from the seed mix. These areas are labeled as Unit 4a on the sagebrush
seedling map and are slated for Wyoming big sagebrush plug planting because of
the 1-mile proximity to leks. This was an adjustment based off input from the Fish
and Wildlife Service (FWS) during a meeting held on September 18, 2017.
Seed Units 4 and 7 will include research plots 1 and 2. The Eastern Oregon
Agricultural Research Center will conduct the study that will implement five
replicate drill row seedings that include non-native, native, non-native mixed with
native, drill with no seed, and a no drill control. The potential for revegetating after
wildfire in Wyoming big sagebrush communities with native species alone is
relatively unknown because it has usually been co-seeded with non-native species
(Boyd and Davies 2010; Davies et al. 2013a; Knutson et al. 2014) or not seeded at
all. In other areas, some work has been done and found that seeding success using
natives has been low because the seed used was not climatically and/or genetically
appropriate. In the meanwhile it is widely understood that non-native bunchgrasses
establish better than native bunchgrasses when they are co-seeded, but non-native
bunchgrasses may have limited the success of co-seeded natives (Boyd and Davies
2010; Knutson et al. 2014). Determining suitability of native vegetation to
revegetate rangelands after wildfire is important because the selection of plant
materials to be seeded is crucial for successful revegetation. To evaluate the
effectiveness of using native vegetation and to provide land managers with
important information to assist them in selecting plant materials for revegetating
sagebrush rangeland after wildfire, it is critical to compare seeding native with nonnative
vegetation.

Planned_Implementation:
This EA proposes to incorporate seeding treatments as a component of the Vale District’s Integrated Invasive Plant
Management. The objective of competitive seeding and planting is to provide a vegetative component to compete with invasive plants in treatment areas where existing native plants are unlikely to establish in sufficient quantity or quickly enough to prevent undesirable vegetation from taking over a site. In compliance with LM’s Integrated Vegetation Management Handbook (USDI 2008a), native plants are given the first consideration for competitive seeding and planting. The Handbook states, “Diverse, healthy, and resilient native plant communities provide the greatest opportunity to be successful in meeting multiple use objectives within BLM. [BLM is required to] set resource management objectives that can be met using native species for most situations. However, as a last resort, it may be necessary to introduce nonnative, non-invasive plant materials to break unnatural disturbance
cycles or to prevent further site degradation by noxious or invasive plants” (USDI 2008a.87)/
Reestablishing vegetation with native seed mixtures can be challenging depending on site conditions. One study in the Great Basin found nearly 50 percent of the sites seeded with native species failed to meet restoration objectives (Hull 1973). Other studies found poor results especially in lower precipitation zones (less than 11 inches annually), lower elevations (less than 4,000 feet), in drought years, and in areas that are already dominated by nonnative perennial grasses and weedy annual grass (i.e. high competition environments) (Knutson et al. 2014). Native seedings are more likely to meet management objectives in higher precipitation zones (greater than 11 inches), at higher elevations, in non-drought years when normal or above normal winter and spring precipitation results in increased germination and establishment, and in areas that had more intact native plant communities that existed prior to the treatment (i.e. not weedy sites).
There are potential treatment areas on the Vale District that have limited ecological site potential or are in such a degraded state that attempting to reintroduce exclusively native plants immediately following invasive plant treatments would be unsuccessful and would not meet the objective of the treatment. These sites tend to be low elevation, dry sites in Malheur County with less than eight inches of annual precipitation or in active or recently vacated mining areas.
Some of the non-invasive, nonnative species like crested wheatgrass are effective competitors against invasive annual grasses, but also can outcompete native species that are sown in the same mix (Knutson et al. 2014) or native grasses and forbs that try to recolonize seeded sites (Miles and Karl 1995, Pellant and Lysne 2005). Areas seeded with nonnative grasses, especially forage species like Siberian and crested wheatgrass have largely been successful but can result in monocultures of nonnative forage grasses, usually with lowered species diversity than what was observed prior to the disturbance.
The development of efforts such as the Great Basin Restoration Initiative (1999) and the Great Basin Native Plant Project (2015) is improving the science and cultural practices of seeding native grasses and forbs and reestablishing shrubs like sagebrush. There is a high probability that native seeding in low elevation low precipitation areas with high levels of invasive annual grasses would continue to have mixed success. However, using selective herbicides like imazapic in these areas will reduce competition of invasive annual grasses and allow the native seed to establish.
Areas burned by wildfire on the Vale District are assessed by an interdisciplinary team to identify whether and where there is a need to implement Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation projects. The assessment includes looking at the need to implement competitive seeding to prevent increases in (or spread from) existing invasive plants. Seeding objectives are identified and multiple factors are assessed to recommend seeding treatment needs. Factors analyzed include burn intensity, vegetative community, and risk of invasive plants. Seed mixes are developed by analyzing the pre-fire vegetation community; adjacent, unburnt vegetation communities; site potential; seed availability; and, annual precipitation. Seeding methods are chosen based on topography, rockiness, accessibility, and size of area to be seeded. These assessment considerations are noted in the Integrated Invasive Plant Management, Competitive Seeding and Planting Methods section of Chapter 2 (see below). The same process would be used before competitive seeding for invasive plant control purposes. Competitive seeding and planting occurs in conjunction with other treatments. Seeding is accomplished with hand spreaders, OHV spreaders, harrows, or drills, or is aerially seeded. Plugs or potted plants are planted using hand tools. Seeding with a rangeland drill entails the use of a tractor to pull a drill featuring a high-clearance reinforced frame, and single-disk openers that are independently suspended on trailing arms. The drill creates a shallow furrow, deposits seed and uses chains to drag soil to cover the seed. The depth of disturbance depends on the type of seed being planted. When drill seeding, it is critical to cover the seed properly and firm the soil once seed is placed between 0.25 and 0.50 inches below the surface (Shewmaker and Bohle 2004). It is difficult to control seed depth and soil firming with broadcast seeding or a harrow, but not all sites are conducive to a rangeland drill operation. To ensure best results when broadcast seeding, increasing the seed rate by 30 to 100 percent is suggested to offset for poorly placed seed. Broadcasting in two directions perpendicular to one another is suggested.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The proposed action is described in the Post-Fire Recovery Plan, Emergency Stabilization and Burned Area Rehabilitation, Bowden Fire (K7ZV), BLM Vale District Office, OREGON STATE OFFICE (hereafter called ESR Plan, July 26, 2017). Specifically, this Determination of National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) Adequacy evaluates proposed actions for emergency stabilization and rehabilitation of burned areas within the Bowden fire. This document evaluates proposed actions in the ESR Plan for adequacy of existing NEPA analyses and conformance with the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS, April 2001) for the Southeastern Oregon Resource Management Plan (SEORMP) Record of Decision (ROD, September 2002) as well as the 2015 FEIS for the Oregon Greater Sage-Grouse RMP (ARMPA, September 2015). In July of 2017, the Bowden fire (project area) burned 16,742 acres within the Bowden Hills Allotment. The fire area is completely within a designated sage-grouse General Habitat Management Area (GHMA). In order to rehabilitate the project area\u2019s native plant community, authorization and implementation of an Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation (ES&R) project occurred in 2017. The ES&R treatments included an aerial application of imazapic in the fall of 2017, followed by aerial and drill seeding of native perennial grass, forb and shrub species in the fall of 2018. In 2019, field visits and monitoring showed success of the seeding treatments as evidence by the establishment of drilled and aerial seeded species, with the west section of the fire having greater success than the northeast section. However, Russian thistle established throughout much of the project area with a dense monoculture of an average of 28 percent cover in the 2,550-acre northeast section due to the lack of established deep-rooted perennial grasses. Resource concerns within the burned area include maintenance of native perennial and desirable non-native plant species and expansion of existing weeds, especially cheatgrass and Russian thistle. Proposed re-treatments and actions include temporary fence construction, livestock grazing closures, herbicide treatment, aerial seeding, and monitoring. Class III cultural surveys were completed during 2017 and 2018; additional surveys would be required prior to any ground disturbing activities that have not been previously surveyed. Project Design Features Project Design Features (PDFs) were developed to aid in meeting project goals and objectives. These features are a component of BLM Adaptive Management process and are subject to change based on site-specific terrain characteristics (topography and vegetation). Changes, additions, or deletions would be made through coordination with appropriate BLM specialists and approved by the Malheur Field Office Manager.

Monitoring Conclusions
Twelve AIM monitoring plots were established in 2019 and were not monitored in 2022.
Two AIM monitoring plots were established in 2020. Both plots (T125-Fairbanks-MAR-20 and T125-LakeCK-MAR-20) are not meeting the perennial cover objective. Both plots are meeting the 3-year ESR objective for density.
Five AIM monitoring plots were established in 2021. The only plot not meeting the 3-year ESR objective for percent perennial cover is T124-A2TwinValley-MAR-21 the rest are meeting the objective. Likewise, two of the sites (WM-Shade-170 and T124-A4Buttermilk-MAR-21) are not meeting the 3-year ESR objectives for density, the rest are meeting the objective.
One major takeaway in the Monitoring Results Summary section is that Sandberg bluegrass was a seeded species that was seen at multiple sites. Thus, it could indicate that Sandberg bluegrass is well established and adapted to these sites, has high vigor and reproductive capability, and may be coming back naturally in addition to the supplemental aerial and drill seeding.

Objectives:
1. Foliar cover of perennial grasses (excluding Sandberg bluegrass) is an average of greater than or equal to 20%.
2. Density of large stature perennial grasses (excluding Sandberg bluegrass) is an average of greater than or equal to 3 plants per m2.
3. Basal diameter of large statured seeded grasses (bluebunch wheatgrass, Snake River wheatgrass, Siberian wheatgrass, and/or crested wheatgrass) has a median value of greater than or equal to 3 inches, excluding Sherman big bluegrass and thickspike wheatgrass.
4. A qualitative assessment of the fitness and vigor of native and seeded perennial plant species determines those species to be established. The assessment would include at a minimum the following factors:
- Seed head and seed production
- Root mass, and lateral and vertical growth
- Precipitation during germination and growing season
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 850 acres of native seed drill seeding.
Actual_Implementation: Native drill seed mix was submitted for purchase in winter 2021 using MO FY21 funds. The initial cultural survey was completed in October 2021, for the proposed drill seeding acres. Site evaluations are still in progress and acreage adjustments will be made after final survey is completed. Approximately 850 acres of native seed was drill seeded in the fall of 2022. Rented a tractor for 2nd drill set up.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
In the summer 2021, baseline monitoring plots were established in the southern parts of the Wildcat fire boundary prior to treatments to better determine the overall success of treatments. The treatments carried out on the southern side included aerial herbicide application of imazapic and drill seeding of native grasses and spiny hop sage (Grayia spinosa). The drill seeding project area covers the toe slope of an alluvial fan that experienced low fire severity (Sentinel Fire Severity: Wildcat ESR 2020 map).

The aerial herbicide application of imazapic in the fall of 2021 reduced cheatgrass foliar cover from 12.2% to 0.4% by summer of 2022 (Table 7-2). The reduction of cheatgrass to 0.4% meets our objective for the first year of the two-year objective for invasive annual grass aerial herbicide treatment. Either due to the fire or ongoing drought conditions, much of the area had a low density of deep-rooted perennial bunchgrasses throughout the treatment area. In 2021, the baseline data showed the area had 1.8% foliar cover for deep-rooted perennial bunchgrasses and shallow-rooted bunch grasses had 0.4% foliar cover prior to drill seeding. Deep-rooted perennial grasses showed no significant change between 2021 and 2022 and continue to be below all objective thresholds (Table 7-1).

In 2023, plots for the drill seeded area were revisited to gauge treatment success. In 2023 the median basal diameter is the only objective being met for the drill seeding. There is a slight increase in the deep-rooted perennial grass density from the previous year due to the new bunchgrasses establishing within the treatment area. There is a trace amount of cheatgrass in the drill seeding area which can be attributed to the aerial herbicide spraying and the rocky soil type. The soil may be influencing the low treatment success for the establishment of bunchgrasses.
